steps.user_message: Here's my situation for 2024 taxes. I'm married filing jointly, live in San Diego CA. My employer Midwest Health Systems paid me $84,900 (W-2). I also earned $8,900 doing graphic design for 4 clients, got $890 interest from Discover Bank savings and $480 dividends from E*TRADE. I work from home in a 100 sq ft office; rent is $2,100/month, total space 850 sq ft. I paid $4,800 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2016–2019), gave $720 to Doctors Without Borders I have the receipt, and had $650 in work supplies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — useful detail. Below is a practical, step‑by‑step summary of what’s deductible, whether you should itemize, how to treat the home office, and which federal forms/worksheets you’ll use. I’ll highlight assumptions and next steps you can ask me to run.

Quick summary (short):
- Likely better to take the federal standard deduction for 2024 (Married Filing Jointly: $29,200) — your likely itemized deductions (charity $720 plus any SALT) are well below that.
- Report the $8,900 graphic‑design income on Schedule C (Form 1040). Deduct the $650 supplies on Schedule C.
- You can claim a home‑office deduction for the self‑employment work space (100 sq ft of an 850 sq ft home → 100/850 = 11.76%). You can use either the simplified method ($5/sq ft → $500) or the regular method (your share of rent/utilities). Regular method will likely give a larger deduction because your rent is $2,100/mo.
- Student loan interest is an above‑the‑line deduction (Form 1040 Schedule 1), but limited to $2,500 max (subject to income phaseouts). With the income you reported, you will likely be able to take the deduction up to the limit if you actually paid $4,800 in 2024 — only $2,500 is deductible.
- Charitable gift ($720): deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A). If you take the standard deduction, you cannot deduct that gift on your federal return.
- Interest ($890) and dividends ($480): report on Form 1040 (Schedule B only required if interest or dividends exceed $1,500 each).
- You will owe self‑employment tax on the net profit from the business and should file Schedule SE; half of that SE tax is deductible on Schedule 1.

Details and recommended treatment

1) Should you itemize or take the standard deduction?
- 2024 federal standard deduction (MFJ) = $29,200.
- Your known itemizable federal deductions:
  - Charitable cash gifts: $720 (you said you have the receipt).
  - Potential state and local taxes (SALT): only deductible up to $10,000 total (state income tax withheld or estimated payments, or property tax/sales tax). You didn’t list state tax payments or property tax, so I can’t add more.
- Even if you max out SALT ($10,000) plus $720 charity = $10,720, that’s far less than $29,200. So most likely take the standard deduction. If you have significant state tax or mortgage interest or large unreimbursed medical expenses that you didn’t list, re‑check — otherwise standard is the better option.

2) Self‑employment income and business expenses
- Put the $8,900 on Schedule C (business income).
- Deduct the $650 supplies directly on Schedule C as business expenses.
- You can also deduct the home‑office amount (see next) on Schedule C.
- You’ll calculate self‑employment tax on Schedule SE (approx. 15.3% on net earnings), and you can deduct half of the SE tax as an adjustment on Schedule 1.
- Keep good records (invoices, bank deposits, receipts). If you received any 1099‑NEC forms from clients, include them.

3) Home office deduction (you work from a 100 sq ft office in an 850 sq ft home)
- Business percentage = 100 / 850 = 11.7647% (≈11.76%).
- Two options:
  - Simplified method: $5 × 100 sq ft = $500. No Form 8829 required.
  - Regular method: allocate real expenses to the business percentage. Example using rent only: annual rent = $2,100 × 12 = $25,200 → 11.7647% × $25,200 ≈ $2,964 for rent portion alone. Add that same percent of utilities, renter’s insurance, etc., if you pay them. You must use Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) to compute the deduction when using the regular method.
- Because your rent is high, the regular method will probably give you a much larger deduction than the simplified method — but it requires supporting records and use of Form 8829.
- Important rules: the space must be used regularly and exclusively for business (exclusive use test), and the deduction cannot exceed your business income from that activity (excess can be carried forward in many cases). Home office deductions are only available for self‑employed people — W‑2 employees cannot claim it under current law.

4) Student loan interest
- Up to $2,500 of student loan interest is an adjustment to income (reported on Form 1040, Schedule 1). You must have paid the interest in the tax year and have the records/Form 1098‑E (or your receipt).
- You reported $4,800 paid — the annual deduction cap is $2,500 (subject to income phaseouts). Based on the wages and self‑employment income you listed, you are likely under the phaseout threshold for MFJ, so you should be able to claim the full $2,500 (confirm with your exact AGI). If you want, I can check phaseout thresholds vs your exact AGI.

5) Interest and dividends
- Report $890 interest and $480 dividends on Form 1040. You don’t need Schedule B unless either category exceeds $1,500 (or certain other conditions apply).

6) Other possible items
- Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction (Section 199A): you may be eligible for up to 20% of qualified business income from your graphic design income after deductions. Whether you can claim it and how much depends on taxable income and whether the business is classified as a specified service. This can be complicated — I can run an estimate if you want.
- Estimated tax payments: if you expect to owe significant self‑employment tax or income tax beyond withholding, consider estimated quarterly payments for next year.

7) Forms and worksheets you’ll use (federal)
- Form 1040 (individual return)
- Schedule 1 (Form 1040): for adjustments to income — student loan interest deduction, half of self‑employment tax adjustment appears here too.
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business): report $8,900 revenue, $650 supplies, home office (either via Form 8829 or simplified entry).
- Schedule SE: compute self‑employment tax.
- Form 8829: Use only if you choose the regular method for the home office deduction.
- Schedule A: only if you decide to itemize (likely not).
- Schedule B: only if interest or dividends > $1,500.
- Keep Form 1098‑E (student loan interest) and any 1099‑NEC/1099‑MISC your clients issued.

State (California)
- File California Form 540 (or 540NR if nonresident). CA rules differ in some ways from federal; confirm whether CA conforms for particular deductions like student loan interest or QBI treatment. If you want, I can note CA specifics after you confirm any state‑tax withholding or property tax amounts.

Practical numbers (examples)
- Home office % = 11.76% (100/850).
- Simplified home office deduction = $500.
- Regular method (rent only) ≈ $2,964 (11.76% × $25,200). Add your utilities, renter’s insurance proportion if you want a fuller number.
- Student loan interest deductible up to $2,500 (not $4,800).

Recordkeeping checklist
- Receipts for charitable donation ($720) and student loan interest payment(s) or 1098‑E.
- Receipts/invoices for supplies ($650).
- Records showing the office is used exclusively for business (photos, floor plan, dated diary entries if needed).
- Rent statements and utility bills to allocate for the regular home office method.
- 1099s and W‑2.

Next steps I can help with
- Run the math: compare tax outcomes using simplified vs regular home office method (I’ll need your annual utilities, renter’s insurance, and any other home expenses and any state tax withholding).
- Estimate your self‑employment tax and total federal tax liability given the numbers you provided and confirm student loan deduction phaseout.
- Prepare a checklist of what to upload to tax software or give to a tax preparer.

Would you like me to:
A) Compare simplified vs regular home office deduction using estimated utilities (I can use a placeholder if you don’t have exact numbers), or
B) Estimate your federal tax/self‑employment tax for 2024 with the numbers you’ve given?

Pick A or B (or tell me what details you want me to compute).
